# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Every grouped answer sits where I would put it, the two group names are plain, and Ravi's board-approval answer rightly stands alone because it is about who signs off, not the fee or the yield.
whys.g2: There is no junk or explicit answer on this line, and Ravi's slightly off-question board answer is kept out of the groups rather than forced into one.

founder.order_why: It runs the way I'd pitch it: who and when, then the problem, then Palus, then who signs and what it costs, then who gets asked, so each step builds on the one before.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so they read as the same screen twice unless the second says what it adds.
founder.missing: No way to state a price as a share of the balance (our 0.25% a year on AUM) or the size of the reserve it applies to, so I had to turn it into a guessed monthly dollar range. The cost question also had no place to say the cost is yield given up rather than money spent.

screens.why2: The question and modes are plain to me, but the helper line 'The part of the long-term reserve they lose' reads like losing principal, which is the bet-the-company fear, when my cost is yield given up; I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: The yield a reserve gives up by sitting in the bank's treasury product is my own pitch number, and I know it per company per year.
screens.why4: Money, time and a share are distinct and cover how the cost could be put, and 'I'm not sure' is the right escape on the founder's side.
screens.why5: My mode, 2%, base 'the long-term reserve', 'per company', 'a year' and my loss line are all kept exactly, and the belief line says what I typed.
screens.why7: One measure, a percent of my base with 'of the long-term reserve' kept; heading payer and belief deciders are the same paying unit in the plural; my per-unit and period are kept, no number is rounded, and the 'I'm not sure' escape is there as the card requires.
screens.instead: Same screen, with the helper under the box changed to 'The yield on the long-term reserve they gave up', so a share they lose is not read as principal lost.

screens.why1: After the cost question and with the founder named as the one who decides, asking my price is the obvious next step in the paying section.
screens.why2: "A percent of the long-term reserve" and "a year" are how I already talk about my fee (0.25% a year on what sits with us), so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: My price is my own number from launch day: a flat 0.25% a year.
screens.why4: The five shapes cover how a treasury product could charge, the percent row fits my AUM fee exactly, and "No price yet" is the right escape.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 0.25%, the yearly period and the base my fee is charged on, and names Palus; "long-term reserve" is a fair plain word for the assets under management.
screens.why7: The percent is of money the payer holds, the base and period are locked from the cost estimate, the belief uses the percent form and names Palus with my whole value, and the escape is No price yet.

screens.why1: Right after the price, asking who besides me has to agree before the company commits its reserve is the obvious next step, and screen 10 only settled that the founder, not the finance lead, decides.
screens.why2: "Besides the startup founder, who has to agree before they can buy?" is plain to me, and "the board" is the first thing that comes to mind for where a company's cash sits.
screens.why3: I know exactly who signs off on moving our treasury, and so does every founder I'd pitch: me, and for a multi-million reserve, often the board or the lead investor.
screens.why4: A free box for up to two roles, with "Nobody" allowed as an answer and "I'm not sure" as the only chip, covers every honest answer I could give.
screens.why5: It names the founder as the decider, as I said on the earlier screen, and leaves the roles to me, so "The board" goes in exactly as I typed it.
screens.why7: The box matches the card's founder list (at most two roles, up to four words each, Nobody as an answer, and "I'm not sure" as the only founder-side escape), so "The board" can become the tested role.

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as the one who has to agree, Keel shows me the roles back to check before it builds the belief, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Finance lead, startup founder and the board are plain words in my world, and the tags (has the problem, decides to buy, has to agree) read on first pass; the only wobble is the intro repeating the title.
screens.why3: I know exactly who moves our cash, who signs off on where the reserve sits, and that our board weighs in on the cash policy.
screens.why4: The rows are complete and distinct: Nobody else fixed first, then the practitioner, the decider and the one role I named, each tagged once, with no role I never typed.
screens.why5: It keeps my split exactly: the finance lead lives it, the founder decides, and the board, the one role I typed, has to agree.
screens.why7: The rows meet the card's shape: Nobody else first and fixed, my one named role kept in my words and tagged has to agree, every row carrying one plain tag, and nothing added. The belief can only read 'The founder decides, and the board must agree first.', which the fixed four can both support and refute.

screens.why1: Right after I named the board and checked Keel's rows, picking which version of who-decides to test is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Nobody else' and 'The board · has to agree' are exactly how I'd say it about where a startup's reserve sits, and the bar reads plainly.
screens.why3: Whether a founder can move the long-term reserve alone or needs the board's nod on the cash policy is something I know first-hand.
screens.why4: Two distinct, complete choices, deciding alone or with the board, and the board row is the one role I named, tagged plainly.
screens.why5: It keeps my word 'The board' and the belief says what I meant: the founder decides, and the board must agree first.
screens.why7: This is the card's good example: the decider alone or with the one role I named, the belief carries the board rather than 'nobody else', and the bar counts sign-off-myself and board-must-agree for, so it can hold or fail.

screens.why1: Right after naming who has to agree, asking what the founder's own side must clear before signing up is the obvious next step in how Palus sells.
screens.why2: 'The buyer's own side' and 'before they pay' read a little abstractly for my sale, where the buyer is a founder and nobody pays upfront: they move the reserve and a 0.25% fee accrues, though the hint and example make it clear on a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what founders hit before moving cash to a new provider: weeks of diligence, a board-approved cash policy and a tax adviser's view on the bonds.
screens.why4: A free box for up to four steps plus a single 'I'm not sure' escape is the right shape, and nothing is missing or odd.
screens.why5: My three steps stand exactly as I typed them, in my order, biggest first.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 buyer-side brakes of up to 9 words, biggest first, excludes my own trial or pilot, defers the time to my own next answer, and offers the card's founder escape 'I'm not sure'.
screens.instead: What must a startup founder's side clear before moving its reserve into Palus? (up to four steps, biggest first, e.g. 'board approval of the cash policy'; not your own trial) · I'm not sure

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree and what the buyer's side must clear, checking the list Keel drafted from my answer is the obvious next step before I pick one and give it a time.
screens.why2: Board approval of the cash policy, diligence on a new provider and a tax adviser's sign-off are how founders and finance leads talk about moving a reserve, so I read each row once and know it.
screens.why3: These are the gates I hear about from every founder I pitch, including the thread's 'it definitely takes weeks to diligence' and 'talk to their tax advisor', so I can judge them from my own sales calls.
screens.why4: Three distinct steps on the buyer's own side, none overlapping, each under 9 words with its object, and none of them is my own offer, pilot or onboarding.
screens.why5: All three are steps I named, in my words, and the screen added no suggested row that drifts from them.
screens.why7: Every row is a brake on the buyer's side that I don't control and none is the purchase itself; 1 to 4 holds, and board approval leads as the gate that can stop the move outright, while the time stays for me to type on the next screen.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the list of steps my buyer's side has to clear, Keel asks me to pick the one to test and say how long I expect it to take; that is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: Diligence on a new provider, board approval of the cash policy and a tax adviser's sign-off are how founders and finance people actually talk about moving a reserve, and the time box asks one plain thing.
screens.why3: I know how long diligence on a treasury provider takes; I've lived it, and commenters told me it 'definitely takes weeks', so 4 weeks is my own number.
screens.why4: The three steps are all mine and distinct (board, provider diligence, tax sign-off on the bonds), the biggest blocker is first, and 'I'm not sure' is the right escape for my side.
screens.why5: Every row is in my words as revised, including 'on the bonds', and the belief carries the step I picked and the 4 weeks I typed.
screens.why7: Each row is a brake on the buyer's side, not my offer or the purchase itself; the time is mine and is the edge; the bar counts under 4 weeks or not needed as support and 4 weeks and longer against, so it can go either way; and the founder-side escape is there.

screens.why1: After who decides, the cost and the friction, the natural next thing I'd want to pin down is the first step I'd ask a founder to take, so it sits right here.
screens.why2: The question asks two things at once, the step and what it costs, and the founder answers in one nine-word line, so I had to read the hint to see the cost goes inside the step as where the money goes.
screens.why3: The first step I'd ask of a founder is my own plan: 'start small, try us out, and grow your position over time'.
screens.why4: The only option is the 'I'm not sure' chip, which is the founder-side escape the card allows, and the free text box takes my own words.
screens.why5: 'Move a small part of the reserve into Palus' is what I would type, and it keeps 'small part', the reserve and my product's name.
screens.why7: The step is nine words in base form after 'would', names what it acts on and where the money goes, keeps 'a small part' and 'Palus', and the hint says a free smaller step follows on the next screen because this one costs money and a signature.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd ask the startup founder to take with Palus, in up to 9 words, saying where any money goes?

screens.why1: After I named my first step and its cost, checking how Keel worded it for strangers, with a free smaller step, is the obvious next screen.
screens.why2: The step is plainly mine, but the smaller-step field reads 'Yes, after a look at Palus on sample data first', a whole framed answer instead of the noun phrase I'm meant to keep or change, so I had to read it twice against the list's 'Probably, after…'.
screens.why3: Whether a founder would move part of the long-term reserve into a new provider is exactly the call I make, and the one founders I pitch make.
screens.why4: Firm yes to the step, a soft yes after a free look, probably not, no: complete, distinct, and in founders' words, with no escape as the card requires.
screens.why5: 'Move a small part of the reserve into Palus' keeps my 'start small' step, the product's name and where the money goes, and the sample-data look is a free first step I can keep.
screens.why7: The served list meets the card: the first option is the step whole, the soft yes is a 'Probably, after {smaller step} first' that costs nothing because moving the reserve costs money and a signature, two answers for and two against, and no escape. But the smaller-step field stores a framed 'Yes, after … first' answer instead of the bare noun phrase, which bends the shape rule.
screens.instead: Your step: move a small part of the reserve into Palus · Or a smaller step first: a look at Palus on sample data · Yes, I'd move a small part of the reserve into Palus / Probably, after a look at Palus on sample data first / Probably not / No

screens.why1: After the commitment step, and just before strangers see the study, it is the obvious point to decide whether to turn yes-sayers into real leads for a first small allocation.
screens.why2: Pilot, email and a Pilot tab are plain to a YC founder, and the two choices read at a glance.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from the founders and finance leads who answer is my own call, and I'm already collecting batchmates who want this.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for a binary choice, and no escape is needed for the founder.
screens.why5: The hint shows a generic 'Would you try this for real?' rather than the step I set, 'move a small part of the reserve into Palus', so I can't tell whether strangers will be asked to start small with real cash or just to try it.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you move a small part of your reserve into Palus to try it? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs at 'before people see it', just before launch, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Two names with a five-second sample and a plain cost (400 credits, same either way) are clear on first read, though the hint is long and says 'voice' where the picked answer says 'face'.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads and founders well enough to hear five seconds and pick a voice they would answer.
screens.why4: The two names are distinct and the preselection works as a default, but the names alone say nothing about tone or accent, so I can only compare them by tapping both.
screens.why5: It says 'finance leads', but my study's buying questions go to founders in Part 3, so the screen names only half of who will hear this voice.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads and founders your questions? Daphne (calm, US accent) ▶ 5 s · Saskia (brisk, US accent) ▶ 5 s. Same 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Choosing a format for the founder link, the one that tests who pays, makes sense here, but it comes straight after I picked one for finance leads, and nothing says this is a second link to different people, so it reads at first like the same question asked twice.
screens.why2: "How should founders answer?" makes me stop for a second because I am a founder myself, and it takes a beat to see it means the startup founders I am asking about paying, not me.
screens.why3: I know my buyers: busy founder-CEOs who will tap through on a phone between meetings. I can pick this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct, cover everything I could want (video, text, or their choice), and each says plainly what the person would do, so no escape option is needed.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed, and nothing about Palus or the finance-lead and founder roles shows through to the people answering.
screens.instead: How should the startup founders, the ones you're asking about paying, answer their questions? (AI interviewer Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: The study is built and sent, so choosing who receives the interview link is the obvious last step before anyone answers.
screens.why2: Named people, a Keel contact list, or one open link posted where people already gather (the batch's forum, a founders' Slack) are plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would reach: the batchmates who told us they wanted this, and the finance leads and ops people I already talk to.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but I would really do two at once (batchmates by name plus one post to the batch), and the screen reads as a single pick with no way to combine them.
screens.why5: Nothing of Palus's product or my wording is changed or leaked here, though the screen does not say whether these links go to the finance leads, the founders, or both.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, finance leads, founders or both? Pick every way you'll reach them: people I know by name (their own link each) / a list I found with Keel / one open link I post where they already are (e.g. the batch forum).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' has a number beside it (1 of 7 lose 2% or more), but the screen calls the page 'the worst of all its cards' and then names Existing sacrifice, while Purchase friction and Commitment read 'Did not hold', which sounds worse, so I cannot tell why that card decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits (e.g. 1 of 7 · bar 5 of 7), but the kicker's '1 TO 8 COUNTED' and Ability to pay's '5 needed' with no bar make me look twice.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are my beliefs. Existing sacrifice says 2%, though my own $50k–75k on $5M is about 1–1.5%. Buyer and payer says the board must agree first, when I tested 'Nobody else'.
screens.why_b4: The status lines say which way each belief missed ('they lose less today than you estimated', 'they value it below your price'), but nothing tells me what to change: the fee, the pitch, or the diligence pack.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and the thin card is called 'too few to call'. But the screen does not say that founders asked what they lost were reporting fees and hours rather than yield given up, so 'they lose less than you estimated' overstates what the answers show.
screens.instead: Not holding up: founders say they lose less than 2% a year today (1 of 7), only 1 of 8 thinks 0.25% fair, and most expect 4 weeks to 3 months of diligence. Lead with a small trial position and a ready diligence pack before defending the fee.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not holding up' sits directly beside '1 of 7 lose 2% or more ... · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it in one line.
screens.why_b2: The axis (0 to 3, % of the long-term reserve a year), the 7 counted and the 5-of-7 bar are all there, but 'your bar' means my 2% on the axis in one place and a 5-of-7 head count on the strip in another, so I had to look twice to see which marker was which.
screens.why_b3: 'About 2% of the long-term reserve per company a year: yield they gave up by leaving the reserve at the bank' is my estimate, base and loss line as I typed them.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points me to the Price card, but it never says what a small felt yield gap means for my pitch, such as leading with the dollar gap on their own balance rather than assuming founders already feel it.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, Ravi's 'couldn't recall' and the two zeros are explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps the verdict from being overstated.
screens.instead: Lean: only 1 of 7 (Maya, 2%) feel they give up 2% of the reserve a year, and the rest put it near zero or about 1%. Most may not see yield left at the bank as a cost, so show founders the dollar gap on their own reserve before you pitch the fee.

screens.why_b1: The card says 'Not holding up' with '1 of 8 at 0.25% or more · bar 6 of 8' right under it, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together and agree.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count and whether it counts for or against, my 0.25% is marked as the low edge of its band, and the strip shows 1 for, 7 against with the marker at 6 of 8, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: 'A fee of 0.25% of the long-term reserve a year fair for Palus' is my flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM in only slightly different words, and founders are who I pitched it to.
screens.why_b4: The So line names where most landed (0.1% to under 0.25%, 3 of 8) but then sends me to the Insights tab instead of saying what it means for my fee, such as that they price it near what their bank's treasury already charges.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the low number is flagged as 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than 1 of 8 can carry.
screens.instead: Fewer than 2 in 3 would pay 0.25%: most put a fair fee between 0.1% and 0.25%, about what their bank's treasury charges now, so test a lower fee or show the yield after fees against the bank's before asking 0.25% (a small group of 8: a lean, not a call).

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits right beside '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know the belief is undecided and the number that keeps it undecided.
screens.why_b2: The strip is plain: one cell for, four ghost cells, the bar at 4 of 5. But the axis '0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5' has no unit, so I can't tell whether it counts people or percent of the reserve without a second look.
screens.why_b3: The 0.25% fee, the long-term reserve and 'paid out of the gain' are recognisably my numbers, but I never typed or checked this sentence; Keel derived it, and the card shows it as my belief.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me the floor, not what to do; the useful message is that only 1 of 8 founders reached 0.25%, so price is what blocks this, not where the money would come from.
screens.why_b5: The small n is said honestly ('a lean, not a call'), but the screen asks where the money would come from and counts by 'loses your price or more'. The So line says Maya 'said where the money would come from', and her row shows her price band, not her loss or her source, so I can't tell what she was counted on.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Maya (of 8) named 0.25% or more, and her reported loss covers it; 7 named less or wouldn't pay, so fix the price before ability to pay can be read.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and its count sit together (Holding up, 7 of 8, bar 6 of 8), but they answer a belief I did not test: I tested *Nobody else*, where only the 5 who could sign alone count for me, which is 5 of 8 under a bar of 6, so not holding.
screens.why_b2: Five could sign, two needed the board, one needed several people and none said someone else's call; the strip shows 7 for and 1 against with the marker at 6 of 8, all readable at first look.
screens.why_b3: My tested line was *Nobody else*, which fits the five-minute pitch; the board was only the other role on my list, yet the card says 'You said the board has to agree' and asks about the board.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the board in most deals' is wrong: only 2 of 8 named the board and 5 of 8 could sign alone, so the line points me the wrong way.
screens.why_b5: It counts the two board answers for me and calls the belief holding up, when on my own belief they count against me and it falls short. The 'lean, not a call' caveat does not fix the flipped verdict.
screens.instead: Nobody else has to agree: not holding up, 5 of 8 could sign alone against a bar of 6 of 8; 2 needed the board and 1 needed several people, so expect a board check in a minority of deals.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each band's founders, the strip shows 8 cells (3 for, 5 against) with the marker at 6, and it labels my 4 weeks as the low edge of the band counted against, so it reads at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The belief uses my own step, "diligence on a new provider", and my own 4 weeks, put to the founders who sign off on where the reserve sits.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a diligence cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months rather than the 4 weeks I assumed, and points me to the Insights tab for what eats that time, which is concrete enough to change how I forecast closing a reserve.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and the card itself calls it "a small group: a lean, not a call"; the only slip is that "longer than your 4 weeks" counts a band that includes exactly 4 weeks, but the chart says so plainly.
screens.instead: The bar line should carry my time as well as my step: "You said diligence on a new provider, about 4 weeks."

screens.why_b1: Did not hold sits right beside 4 of 8 said yes, bar 6 of 8, 2 short, so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts one answer per founder over 8 people, and the strip marks my bar at 6, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Move a small part of the reserve into Palus is my step word for word, and the founder as the one who decides is my framing.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 4 of 8 would not and sends me to the Insights tab, without saying what a split on even a small first step means for how I sell Palus.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, and nothing is claimed past the 4 for and 4 against.
screens.instead: Half of the founders would move a small part of the reserve into Palus today, but nobody took the softer sample-data look, and 4 refused outright, which is 2 short of your bar; with 8 people this is a lean, so find out what the 4 objected to before you lean on a start-small pitch.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding count right under it (Price 1 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction 3 of 8, Commitment 4 of 8), so I know where each line stands.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked: the 0.25% fee on the long-term reserve, diligence within about 4 weeks, and moving a small part of the reserve into Palus.
screens.why_b4: The Price themes hint at the moves (show the net yield after fees, price near what the bank's treasury takes, get the board comfortable with agency MBS), but the screen never says so, and the Friction and Commitment boxes are empty headings with nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: Every box shows how many were against, how many were asked here and who never saw the question, so nothing claims more than the eight founders who answered.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that the fee objection is really about net yield and board comfort with mortgage bonds ('worth a few hundred a month at most' until then), or that a lead investor needed two board calls, and that changes how I'd pitch it.
screens.instead: Say it plainly under Price: founders weigh the fee against the one-point gain and against the bank's fee, and the board has to be comfortable with mortgage bonds first, so lead with the net-of-fee yield and a board-ready memo. Put Felix's 'watch it on paper first' and Ravi's 'two board calls' under Commitment and Purchase friction, where they answer the question.

screens.why1: An idea card is expected before the buying questions, but as the very first thing I hear, with no question about where our raise sits, it lands cold with nothing to anchor it to.
screens.why2: Treasury account, money market fund and Plaid are my words, but 'short-duration, floating-rate' mortgage bonds and 'regulated custodian' are a stack of bond-desk terms I'd need a second read to take in.
screens.why3: Where the raise sits and what it earns against our Mercury treasury sweep is exactly what I decide.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: 'Your long-term reserve' assumes I already split off a pot I won't touch; I'd say 'the cash we won't need for a year or more', so the founder's own framing comes through as if it were mine.
screens.why6: It can be said, with no parenthesis or slash, but the how runs to five sentences and 'short-duration, floating-rate and government-backed' plus 'one to two' and 'four and a half to five percent' is too much to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account for the cash you won't need for a year or more. It puts that cash in government-backed bonds held in your company's name, and you can move it back to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn four and a half to five percent, against about three and a half from a money market fund.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what idle cash already costs us is the obvious place to start the buying questions.
screens.why2: I never went without any of my reserve, since the money is all still there; what I gave up was interest, so 'go without' leaves me guessing what the percent is a percent of.
screens.why3: I know roughly what Mercury pays against a treasury fund on the money we won't touch for a year, but I'd be guessing to turn that into the share this asks for.
screens.why4: One percent box, None and I can't recall are a workable set, but None next to a percent box reads oddly when I can't tell what the percent measures.
screens.why5: The founder's cost is interest given up on idle cash, and 'go without' has drifted into sounding like the reserve itself was lost.
screens.why6: It is short and has one escape, but the spoken label 'A percent of the long-term reserve last year' is a dangling fragment that doesn't say well.
screens.why7: The box keeps the founder's percent of the reserve per year, so answers can be placed against the low, but it uses the vague verb 'go without' that the card says to avoid.
screens.instead: Last year, about what percent of your long-term reserve did you give up in interest by leaving it in the operating account? [box] % of the reserve last year, or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and what I gave up on idle cash, asking what fee I'd accept is the obvious next thing, and I'm the one who signs it off.
screens.why2: Percent fees on balances are how my treasury world talks, but 'the long-term reserve' isn't my phrase; I'd say the cash we won't touch for a year or more, so I'd read it twice to be sure what base the fee is on.
screens.why3: I already pay our bank a treasury fee and I know what I'd tolerate on idle cash, so I can answer this from my own books.
screens.why4: Five clean, non-overlapping percent bands, a refusal option, and 'I can't say' apart cover every answer I'd give.
screens.why5: Nothing of a pitch leaks past the idea card, but 'long-term reserve' reads like the builder's own label for my cash rather than a word I use.
screens.why6: Four short spoken options with the percents said in words, then a two-way follow-up, are easy to hold and answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: Every rung is a percent of money I hold, there are six rungs with 'to under' and 'or more' done right, both sides are present, and the single escape is there.
screens.instead: Palus takes a yearly fee on the cash it holds for you. What fee a year would feel fair to you? Under 0.1% · 0.1% to under 0.25% · 0.25% to under 0.5% · 0.5% to under 1% · 1% or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I named a fee, asking what would make Palus worth more to me is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It reads my band back the way I'd put it, as a percent a year on the reserve, and 'worth more' is plain to me as someone who pays a treasury fee.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make me pay more, like same-day liquidity, insured or Treasury-backed holdings, or less work than my bank's sweep, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It uses the name from the idea card and my own price answer, and nothing new about the founder's plan leaks through.
screens.why6: Read aloud, '0.1% to 0.25%' becomes 'zero point one percent to zero point two five percent', a mouthful, when the guideline says a percent is said in words, like 'a tenth to a quarter of a percent'.
screens.instead: You said about a tenth to a quarter of a percent a year for Palus. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: After the fee I said would feel fair, asking whether I can move the reserve into Palus on my own or need the board is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Sign off and the board are how I talk about moving our raise money, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who has to bless where our treasury sits; it is my call with the board looking over it.
screens.why4: Four distinct steps from me alone to someone else's call, in plain words, with I can't say as the right escape.
screens.why5: The founder named the board and the question names the board; nothing else of their plan leaks beyond the idea I was shown.
screens.why6: Short and holdable, but the stem has no price in it, so I hear sign off on Palus without knowing what amount or fee I am signing for.
screens.why7: Measure, order, the board in the second option and the escape all fit, but the card's item puts the price into the stem and this one drops it.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about 0.25% of the reserve a year for Palus yourself, or would the board have to agree? I could sign off myself; The board would have to agree; Several people would have to agree; It's someone else's call; or I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether the board must agree, asking how long vetting a new place to park our cash would take is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Diligence on a new provider is how I talk about vetting where our raise sits, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I just moved cash between Mercury sweeps and a T-bill account, so I know how long the checks on a new provider take us.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and don't overlap, my real answer of a couple of weeks is there, and I can't tell fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of how Palus works leaks beyond the name I was already shown, and diligence on a new provider is a step on my side.
screens.why6: Short question, four options said once, then a two-way pick, which I can hold by ear without trouble.
screens.why7: The measure, the six bands with an edge at 4 weeks, the balance and the escape all fit, but 4 weeks sits on the ladder's 1 month rung rather than replacing a point, so I cannot tell if it is the founder's own typed time.

screens.why1: It's the last commercial question after price, sign-off and diligence, so asking whether I'd actually move money is the natural close.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but 'a look at Palus on sample data' is software-demo talk; for a treasury account I'd want to see the actual holdings, yields and custody, not 'sample data'.
screens.why3: I decide where our raise sits, so whether I'd move part of the reserve is exactly my call.
screens.why4: The four are complete and distinct with a firm and a soft answer on each side, but the soft yes's 'sample data' is an odd thing to try first with a bond account.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'small part of the reserve' and the product's name, and nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was shown on purpose.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four options I can hold, said as a clean list; the soft yes is a little long but still says well.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's own costly step whole, the soft yes is a free smaller step before it, there are two answers for and two against, and there is no escape, as the card requires.
